<<20:12 update 1, part 0 of 0..3>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
20:12/q01 How is إني read and construed after the call? [إِنِّىٓ · readings] (turns on: Whether the particle begins direct speech or is syntactically governed by the call; the final yāʾ also varies.)
  20:12/q01/p1 Kasra: direct quoted speech after Moses was called. — reasons: Al-Tabari prefers it because يا موسى intervenes; al-Farisi cites the ensuing direct quotations at 20:13–14. Basrans posit an omitted قول; Kufans treat نادى as speech. Abu Ubayd chooses the common reading. Nafi opens the final yāʾ while other kasra readers generally quiet it; the two Medinese readers, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr open it in the five annexed yāʾs enumerated by Ibn al-Jazari.
  20:12/q01/p2 Fatḥa: a subordinate statement giving the content or cause of the call. — reasons: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, also Abu Jafar in several lists, read annī; the yāʾ is open. Al-Zajjaj gives the clause accusative position; others supply bi with نودي, supported by a poetic ناديت باسم example. Ibn Atiyya allows causal 'because'; al-Samin finds it weak, and al-Alusi finds the intervening vocative awkward. Al-Alusi instead supplies أعلم. Qiraat-ER offers 'Know that I am your Lord'. Ibn al-Jazari finds no explicit report for inferring Abu Jafar's yāʾ vowel. Al-Farisi adds that neither quoted clause can serve as deputy subject of passive نودي; the earlier Moses can.
20:12/q02 What grammatical role does أنا play? [أَنَا۠ · grammar]
  20:12/q02/p1 It can be a subject, an emphasis, or a separator. — reasons: Al-Samin says it may be a subject with ربك as predicate, an emphasis of the first-person pronoun, or a separator.
20:12/q03 Why repeat the first-person pronoun in إني أنا ربك? [إِنِّىٓ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكَ · rhetoric]
  20:12/q03/p1 The repetition confirms the speaker's identity and removes Moses' doubt. — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari calls it strengthened proof and secure recognition; Ibn al-Jawzi compares 15:89. Al-Tabarsi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and Bursevi likewise stress certainty.
20:12/q04 Why say 'your Lord' here? [رَبُّكَ · rhetoric]
  20:12/q04/p1 It marks a direct, personal audience with Moses and fits this sura's focus on his worship and mission. — reasons: Tabatabai contrasts the later 'I am Allah,' which states the revealed message. Al-Samarrai contrasts al-Naml and al-Qasas, which say 'Lord of the worlds'; Ta Ha directly instructs Moses in worship and prayer, promises signs and recounts his life.
20:12/q05 How did Moses know who was speaking? [إِنِّىٓ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكَ · theology] (turns on: Whether revelation itself supplies certainty or Moses needs an inferential sign.)
  20:12/q05/p1 God gave Moses immediate, necessary certainty in revelation. — reasons: Al-Alusi favors knowledge created in Moses without inference. Tabatabai says a prophet's initial revelation is directly certain; 42:51 frames divine communication, and rational proof would make prophecy an acquired inference.
  20:12/q05/p2 He inferred divine identity from a miracle or distinctive signs. — reasons: The Mu'tazila require a miracle because necessary knowledge would remove moral responsibility; al-Alusi records prior or later miracle views and questions whether unique-sounding attributes alone withstand satanic suggestion. A report from Wahb says the omnidirectional voice and God's nearness assured Moses; other reports describe hearing from all six directions and through all his limbs, or an unchanged sound regardless of distance.
20:12/q06 How was God's speech heard by Moses? [إِنِّىٓ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكَ · theology] (turns on: The nature of divine speech and whether an audible form is direct, created, or a representation of inner speech.)
  20:12/q06/p1 Moses heard God's own eternal verbal speech directly, without an intermediary. — reasons: A Sunni group in al-Alusi says successive letters need temporal sequence only with an organ such as a tongue; without one the speech can be heard at once.
  20:12/q06/p2 He heard created sound in the tree, while God's speech remains eternal. — reasons: Al-Alusi attributes this to Sunni scholars of Transoxiana.
  20:12/q06/p3 The divine verbal speech was originated. — reasons: Groups al-Alusi calls innovators differ over whether events can subsist in God; those denying this locate the created sound in a body.
  20:12/q06/p4 He spiritually received inner speech that was later represented as words. — reasons: Al-Ashari describes hearing beyond letters, sound and rational comprehension; another account compares familiar word forms produced in intellect and common sense to a dream. Al-Baydawi likewise says spiritual reception is then represented bodily without fixed organ or direction.
20:12/q07 Can this command coexist with eternal divine speech? [فَٱخْلَعْ · theology] (turns on: Whether an eternal command can have an addressee who comes to exist later.)
  20:12/q07/p1 An eternal imperative to Moses before his existence is absurd. — reasons: The Mu'tazila compare it to addressing absent people in an empty house.
  20:12/q07/p2 God's speech is eternal but was not an imperative or prohibition in eternity. — reasons: Al-Razi reports this first reply from his school.
  20:12/q07/p3 The eternal speech is already an order, and Moses later becomes its addressee without a change in it. — reasons: Al-Razi's school compares eternal divine power yielding capacity for action later.
20:12/q08 How does ف connect the sandal command to the declaration? [فَٱخْلَعْ · grammar]
  20:12/q08/p1 The command follows as a consequence of the declaration of God's lordship. — reasons: Al-Alusi says the preceding self-identification motivates removing the sandals.
20:12/q09 What do اخلع and نعل mean literally? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · meaning]
  20:12/q09/p1 The command is to take off the two coverings of Moses' feet. — reasons: Al-Wahidi gives khalaʿ as remove and naʿl as a foot covering; Abu Hayyan says it can be leather, iron, or wood. Al-Alusi notes naʿl is feminine, gives its diminutive, and cites al-Farra's poetry for an alternate vowel on its second radical.
20:12/q10 What were Moses' sandals made of? [نَعْلَيْكَ · reports] (turns on: Whether the footwear was impure donkey hide, pure cowhide, or divinely created.)
  20:12/q10/p1 They were made of hide from an unritually dead donkey, often said to be untanned. — reasons: Qatada, Ka'b, Ali, Ikrima and others transmit it; Ibn Masud attributes a report to the Prophet. Al-Tabari says that report's chain needs scrutiny; al-Tirmidhi calls it gharīb and al-Qurtubi distinguishes the weak Kufan Humayd ibn Ali from trustworthy Meccan Humayd ibn Qays. Al-Alusi calls the transmitted report unusual. Some say donkey hide without specifying carrion.
  20:12/q10/p2 They were ritually pure or slaughtered cowhide. — reasons: Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others give this alternative; Kashifi explicitly prefers processed cowhide.
  20:12/q10/p3 God created the sandals. — reasons: Abu Hayyan records this report along with Moses casting them beyond the valley.
20:12/q11 Why was Moses told to remove the sandals? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the command responds to impure footwear, direct contact with blessing, reverent decorum, or the end of a practical need.)
  20:12/q11/p1 Their dead-animal hide was impure and should not enter the sacred valley. — reasons: Al-Muqatil, Ka'b, Qatada and others identify carrion donkey hide. Al-Tabari objects that neither Quran nor authoritative report establishes this; the verse itself grounds the order in the valley's sanctity. Al-Razi notes tanning would purify hide under a Prophetic ruling, raising an abrogation issue if carrion was the reason.
  20:12/q11/p2 His bare feet should touch and receive the holy ground's blessing. — reasons: Sa'id likens this to entering the Kaaba barefoot; Ibn Abi Najih, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others stress direct contact. Ka'b combines this with donkey hide; al-Hasan and others instead cite pure cowhide. Al-Tabari prefers this because the command is linked to sanctity, without sound proof for impurity. Abu Sufyan says Moses' feet also blessed the valley. Bursevi says the exchange of blessing is mutual.
  20:12/q11/p3 Bare feet express humility and reverence before God or the sacred place. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer royal-court etiquette and say the sandals' substance does not matter; al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the Quran as honoring the place. Al-Razi cites the following valley clause; early Muslims' barefoot circumambulation, Sa'id's Kaaba analogy, Malik's reverence for Medina, Bishr al-Hafi's bare feet and Abu Hanifa's contrasting royal-carpet anecdote illustrate decorum. Islahi adds cleanliness and decency; Kuranyolu sees spiritual preparation for revelation.
  20:12/q11/p4 The sandals' protection against dirt and insects was no longer needed in the pure, safe valley. — reasons: Abu Muslim says God reassured Moses that the place was pure and he was safe.
20:12/q12 What did Moses do with the sandals? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · reports]
  20:12/q12/p1 He removed them and cast them behind or beyond the valley. — reasons: Al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and al-Alusi transmit this detail; Qatada says he then approached.
20:12/q13 What inward act do the two sandals represent? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · inward] (turns on: The symbolic referents proposed for the paired sandals and how far a figurative reading may go.)
  20:12/q13/p1 Cast off attachment to both this world and the next to devote oneself wholly to God. — reasons: Al-Qushayri, al-Razi, Bursevi, al-Ghazzali and Sufi transmitters give this; Ibn Ajibah calls the two sandals realms of existence and the removal a way to witness the Existentiator. Al-Alusi calls the allegory remote. Study Quran notes the sandals' later Sufi poetic and literary use, including Ibn Qasi's Taking Off the Sandals.
  20:12/q13/p2 Set aside family, possessions, livelihood, self and bodily nature. — reasons: Ibn Ata turns the heart away from the created world or l

ower self; dream interpretations associate sandals with wife and child. Bursevi reports wife and sheep and Sheikh Aftade's nature, self and livelihood; Biqai adds that Moses settles without turning back toward family. Al-Alusi includes family and wealth but calls this remote.
  20:12/q13/p3 Shed spiritual states, actions, and one's own attributes before God. — reasons: Al-Shibli speaks of shedding everything of oneself; Ibn Ata names separation and connection. Al-Qushayri adds nearness and distance, union and separation, annihilation and subsistence; Qashani describes effacing attributes and acts in the sacred realm.
  20:12/q13/p4 Leave behind the two proofs or premises once direct knowledge of God is reached. — reasons: Al-Razi and Bursevi give this analogy; Rumi's roof and polished-mirror verses and the king's letter illustrate why further proof is needless. Al-Shibli washing his books makes the same point.
  20:12/q13/p5 The command is a broad metonymy for total devotion. — reasons: Al-Burhan describes a metonymic mode whose whole sentence conveys a gist beyond the surface. Al-Razi objects that this opens the door to esoteric readings that erase the actual sandal command.
20:12/q14 What does Ṭuwā signify in an inward reading of the valley? [بِٱلْوَادِ ٱلْمُقَدَّسِ طُوًۭى · inward]
  20:12/q14/p1 It is the purified spiritual realm or Divine Presence where worldly existence is folded away. — reasons: Al-Qushayri says the valley and divine precinct are free of defects; Qashani calls it the spirit-world with material stages folded beneath it. Ibn Ajibah calls it the inner sanctuary and Ocean of Divine Presence where Moses' soul is enwrapped. Sulami's wordplay says disobedience is folded from his heart.
20:12/q15 Does the sandal command govern prayer or mosque footwear? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · law] (turns on: Whether Moses' occasion-specific command supplies a general rule for worship footwear.)
  20:12/q15/p1 It gives no general objection to praying or circumambulating in clean sandals. — reasons: Al-Razi says the valley's honor made the order specific; the Prophet prayed in sandals, removed them only after Gabriel reported soil, and questioned those who imitated him. Ibn Masud rebuked Abu Musa's imitation and recalled prayer in socks and sandals. Al-Qurtubi cites 7:31 on adornment to support clean sandals and al-Nakhai's wish that removed shoes go to the needy. Al-Alusi notes reports favoring footwear.
  20:12/q15/p2 Shoes should be removed in mosques for cleanliness, humility and decorum. — reasons: Islahi treats this as mandatory and rejects the claim that clean shoes are permitted; Study Quran compares removing shoes before entering the Kaaba or a mosque.
  20:12/q15/p3 Clean shoes may be worn in a mosque. — reasons: Islahi reports this view and rejects it because even clean shoes breach mosque decorum.
20:12/q16 Where should removed sandals be placed during prayer? [نَعْلَيْكَ · law] (turns on: Whether between the feet is acceptable and how to avoid bothering neighboring worshippers.)
  20:12/q16/p1 Between one's feet, without inconveniencing others. — reasons: Abu Hurayra reports a Prophetic instruction and repeats it to al-Maqburi.
  20:12/q16/p2 Ahead of a follower, while left placement is for an imam or one praying alone. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi says a follower should avoid harming the person on his left and places them ahead rather than between the feet.
  20:12/q16/p3 Between the feet is an innovation. — reasons: Jubayr ibn Mut'im says this.
20:12/q17 How are impurities removed from sandals? [نَعْلَيْكَ · law] (turns on: Which impurities rubbing can remove and when washing remains necessary.)
  20:12/q17/p1 Rubbing or scraping can purify leather sandals, including disputed animal impurities. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi prefers rubbing for leather socks and sandals, citing Abu Sa'id's report. Al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr allow earth-rubbing generally for the disputed animal filth; Malikis differ. Abu Hanifa allows scraping dried filth but requires washing wet filth, including urine.
  20:12/q17/p2 Water is required to remove the listed impurities. — reasons: Al-Shafi'i requires water for all; Malik, al-Shafi'i and most jurists agree that blood, human excrement and urine need washing. Abu Hanifa also requires washing when filth is wet.
20:12/q18 What does المقدس mean? [ٱلْمُقَدَّسِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the adjective emphasizes purification or blessing; some sources combine them.)
  20:12/q18/p1 Purified and set apart from impurity or evil. — reasons: Qutrub and Ibn Atiyya give 'purified'; al-Qurtubi derives it from quds, purity, and relates holy land to God removing unbelievers and settling believers. Bursevi adds separation from evil; Biqai says the precinct is purified of what is unfit for a king's court.
  20:12/q18/p2 Blessed, with divine favor and abundance. — reasons: Yahya ibn Sallam, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid give this gloss; Tabarsi specifies ample provision and fertility. Al-Tabari combines purified and blessed, as does al-Nasafi.
20:12/q19 Why is this valley sacred? [بِٱلْوَادِ ٱلْمُقَدَّسِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the ground's holiness follows a specific divine association or the land's purification alone.)
  20:12/q19/p1 God specially favored it through His call, revelation or prescribed worship there. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi says God can favor places, times and creatures; merely removing unbelievers cannot explain this valley's distinct holiness. Tabatabai says places and times have no intrinsic rank, gaining sanctity by noble event or worship. Islahi likewise says all earth is equal in itself and special association with God confers sacredness. Asad ties double holiness to the voice and Moses' prophetic appointment.
  20:12/q19/p2 It was purified by removal of unbelievers and settlement of believers. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi gives this etymological account of the holy land, then says it alone cannot explain this particular valley's sanctity.
20:12/q20 Where is Ṭuwā and what is the valley like? [بِٱلْوَادِ طُوًۭى · referent] (turns on: The differing geographical identifications and physical descriptions.)
  20:12/q20/p1 It is a deep, rounded valley. — reasons: Al-Dahhak likens it to a well; al-Tha'labi records its circular depth.
  20:12/q20/p2 It is in Palestine. — reasons: Al-Hasan locates the twice-sanctified valley there.
  20:12/q20/p3 It is at Aylah. — reasons: Mubashshir ibn Ubayd calls it a valley there, blessed twice and read without nunation.
  20:12/q20/p4 It is at the base of Sinai. — reasons: Islahi describes it as a broad plain at Sinai's base.
  20:12/q20/p5 It is in Syria. — reasons: Al-Jawhari identifies Ṭuwā as a Syrian place name.
  20:12/q20/p6 It is by the mountain where Moses stood. — reasons: Ibn Zayd says Moses received what God gave him at this valley near the mountain.
20:12/q21 What does Ṭuwā mean here? [طُوًۭى · meaning] (turns on: Whether Ṭuwā is a place name, a doubled sanctification or call, an act of treading or crossing, a night expression, or a personal name.)
  20:12/q21/p1 It is the proper name of the valley. — reasons: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others identify it as a name; Ibn Zayd calls it ancient. Al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi prefer this. Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi take it as appositional clarification; it appears also at 79:16. The name can still be explained by doubled sanctity, and spellings vary.
  20:12/q21/p2 It means twice or repeatedly: the valley was sanctified or blessed twice. — reasons: Qatada, al-Hasan and others report double blessing. Al-Farisi notes thanā denotes a repeated occurrence; Ibn al-Sayyid derives Ṭuwā from folding twice. Adi ibn Zayd's poetry supports ṭawā for repetition, though transmitters also read thanā. Asad favors this sense because God spoke there and Moses became a prophet; some make the repeated event two divine calls instead of doubled sanctity.
  20:12/q21/p3 It tells Moses to tread or traverse the valley, especially barefoot. — reasons: Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and Sa'id transmit this; Sa'id likens bare feet in Ṭuwā to entering the Kaaba. Some describe Moses crossing the valley by night and ascending its upper part, deriving the sense from folding or crossing a valley.
  20:12/q21/p4 It denotes the night hour when Moses was called. — reasons: Qutrub makes it an adverb of المقدس; al-Kirmani reportedly calls it an Arabized word for night. Al-Tha'labi includes a derivation from night.
  20:12/q21/p5 It is a man's Hebrew name, used as a vocative. — reasons: Al-Alusi records this as an isolated interpretation.
20:12/q22 How is Ṭuwā pronounced? [طُوًۭى · readings] (turns on: The initial vowel, tanwīn, and in one reported form the word's consonants.)
  20:12/q22/p1 With ḍamma and tanwīn, fully declined. — reasons: The Kufans and Ibn Amir are repeatedly named; Asim, Hamza and al-Kisai are included, and al-Suyuti records Asim's form. It is commonly parsed as a masculine valley or place name. Al-Tabari prefers tanwīn because it also fits a verbal noun. Al-Farra notes this may be indeclinable in some analyses.
  20:12/q22/p2 With ḍamma and no tanwīn. — reasons: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr and Abu Jafar are named. Al-Nahhas prefers nondeclension, as does Ibn Khalawayh for the verse endings. Analyses include a feminine region name, a shifted proper name like Umar, foreignness, or land-name analogy with Hunayn and Hira. This reading appears at 79:16 too.
  20:12/q22/p3 With kasra and tanwīn. — reasons: Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal and Ibn Muhaysin are named. Al-Zajjaj likens its declension to ma'an or dil'; some explain the form as repeated sanctification.
  20:12/q22/p4 With kasra and no tanwīn. — reasons: Abu Zayd reports this from Abu Amr; Ikrima is associated with kasra. It may be an uninflected place-name, as al-Farra's Hunayn and Hira analogies illustrate.
  20:12/q22/p5 Ṭāwī instead of Ṭuwā. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports a group reading بالواد المقدس طاوي; al-Samin attribute

s طاوي اذهب to Isa ibn Umar and al-Dahhak.
20:12/q23 How does Ṭuwā function grammatically? [طُوًۭى · grammar] (turns on: Whether Ṭuwā is a place-name appositive, an elliptical clarification, a verbal noun, or an adjective; its inflection reflects its analysis.)
  20:12/q23/p1 It is an apposition or explanatory apposition to الوادي. — reasons: Al-Tabari makes the proper name genitive by apposition; al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi agree. Al-Samin lists apposition or badal.
  20:12/q23/p2 It is supplied as a nominative subject or accusative clarification. — reasons: Al-Samin permits a nominative with implied subject or an accusative with implied أعني.
  20:12/q23/p3 It is a verbal noun or adjective of repeated sanctification, or attached to the call. — reasons: Al-Hasan uses a verbal noun from folding twice; al-Farisi allows an adjective like thanā and sawā; al-Alusi attaches it to المقدس or نودي. Al-Nahhas cites a hadith against double collection as part of the double-folding analysis.
  20:12/q23/p4 Its declension depends on masculine name, feminine locality, shifted form, foreignness or regional status. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj gives four forms and contrasts masculine fu'al, feminine place-name and shifted name; Ibn Khalawayh questions the proposed unattested Ṭāwin, while al-Farisi allows analogy without one. Al-Farra compares Hunayn and Hira. Al-Samin and al-Alusi add foreignness; tanwīn may also fit a verbal noun.
20:12/q24 Is the final yāʾ of الوادي pronounced? [بِٱلْوَادِ · readings]
  20:12/q24/p1 It may be restored or omitted without changing the meaning. — reasons: Qiraat-ER notes a ten-reader restored yāʾ and a shortened form following the rasm. Ibn al-Jazari documents deletion and restoration at both بالواد المقدس occurrences, الواد الأيمن and وادي النمل, with routes differing for al-Kisai.
20:12/q25 What connects this wording to other Quranic accounts? [* · links]
  20:12/q25/p1 It recalls the call from the tree at 28:30 and the staff sign at 7:117. — reasons: Al-Tabarsi marks those links; Study Quran also reports God called from a tree. Al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi refer back to discussion of the sacred land at 5:21. Al-Farisi compares 79:16–17 for Ṭuwā's reading; the direct-address wording is contrasted with al-Naml and al-Qasas by al-Samarrai.
20:12/q26 What is reported about the tree and the call's visible setting? [* · reports] (turns on: The distinct reports about the tree, fire, voice and Moses' experience.)
  20:12/q26/p1 A green tree blazed with white fire without burning and angels glorified God. — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari adds great light, Moses' fright and calm, and calls the tree buckthorn; al-Tabarsi stresses that green and fire did not extinguish one another. Study Quran reports lycium or boxthorn.
  20:12/q26/p2 The tree moved away as Moses approached, then nearer when he turned back. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq's report says God spoke after this movement.
  20:12/q26/p3 The caller came from a tree. — reasons: Al-Tabarsi connects this to 28:30; Study Quran reports this identification.
  20:12/q26/p4 The sight or call is associated with the fire, which consumed the tree. — reasons: Study Quran transmits this alternate identification and cites 20:10.
  20:12/q26/p5 The call enveloped Moses from every direction. — reasons: Ja'far says each hair perceived it and divine majesty stunned him; al-Zamakhshari records hearing with every limb. Wahb says God was above, with, before and behind Moses and nearer than himself.
20:12/q27 How is the fiery encounter understood inwardly? [* · inward]
  20:12/q27/p1 Divine light and love consumed Moses' selfhood and revealed God through a fiery veil. — reasons: Qashani calls the fire a curtain of majesty and the declaration a veiled manifestation. Bursevi reads light as love and fire as ardent love, burning away selfhood. Ja'far says Moses was annihilated before an address borne and answered by God.
20:12/q28 What does the verse show about God and place? [* · theology]
  20:12/q28/p1 The divine speaker is not contained by the valley or by time. — reasons: Biqai says the purified courtly setting also signals transcendence of spatial and temporal containment.
  20:12/q28/p2 The divine manifestation may be veiled in created fiery form. — reasons: Qashani treats 'I am your Lord' as manifestation behind fiery curtains of majesty.
20:12/q29 What is the scope of figurative interpretation here? [* · interpretation]
  20:12/q29/p1 A metonymic reading can convey the whole sentence's gist beyond its apparent words. — reasons: Al-Burhan describes this rhetorical mode; al-Razi objects that it could turn the real sandal order into mere total devotion, opening boundless esoteric reinterpretation.
20:12/q30 What is said here about the preceding divine istiwāʾ? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether istiwāʾ denotes power or an independently named act or attribute.)
  20:12/q30/p1 The sounder interpretation is divine power. — reasons: Al-Jishumi prefers Abu Ali's view and calls the Kullabi account of an act or attribute named istiwāʾ unintelligible.
  20:12/q30/p2 It is a divine act or attribute called istiwāʾ. — reasons: Al-Jishumi reports this Kullabi position only to argue against it.
20:12/q31 Who identifies himself to Moses in this address? [إِنِّىٓ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكَ · interpretation]
  20:12/q31/p1 God himself is the speaker addressing Moses. — reasons: Ibn Kathir takes the words as God's explicit self-identification.
20:12/q32 What legal status does untanned carrion leather have? [نَعْلَيْكَ · law]
  20:12/q32/p1 It is impure, with two noted dissenters. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi says jurists generally agree that untanned dead-animal leather is impure, except al-Zuhri and al-Layth.
20:12/q33 What court custom is used to explain taking off the sandals? [فَٱخْلَعْ نَعْلَيْكَ · interpretation]
  20:12/q33/p1 Shoes are removed when entering a king's court. — reasons: Al-Qushayri reports this as an analogy for Moses' presence before God.
20:12/q34 How does the ruling on tanning affect the carrion-hide explanation? [نَعْلَيْكَ · law]
  20:12/q34/p1 The later Prophetic ruling purifies tanned hide and would abrogate an earlier ban if that ban explained Moses' removal. — reasons: Al-Razi cites the Prophet's saying that any tanned hide becomes pure.
20:12/q35 How has the sandal image appeared in Sufi literature? [نَعْلَيْكَ · inward]
  20:12/q35/p1 It became a recurring image in poetry and named works. — reasons: Study Quran notes Ibn Qasi's book Taking Off the Sandals among its literary afterlives.
20:12/q36 What root is Ṭuwā derived from? [طُوًۭى · meaning]
